question: A documentation team is iterating on a prompt that generates article summaries. They have 250 articles paired with human-written reference summaries and want an automated score that rewards a candidate summary for preserving the key information from the reference in a similar order, so they can compare prompt variants at scale during iteration. Which evaluation method best fits this need?
options: A) Score each candidate summary against its reference using ROUGE-L and track the F1 score across prompt variants
B) Measure the wall-clock latency of each prompt variant and prefer whichever version returns a response fastest
C) Compute exact string match between the candidate summary and the reference summary for each article
D) Ask a separate Claude call to output a single yes/no verdict on whether the summary mentions any protected health information
correct_answers: A) Score each candidate summary against its reference using ROUGE-L and track the F1 score across prompt variants
explanations: Correct. ROUGE-L measures the longest common subsequence between candidate and reference text, capturing whether key information appears in a similar order, and it is well suited to scoring summarization quality across many articles automatically.
Incorrect. Latency measures response speed, not whether the generated content faithfully reflects the reference summary's content.
Incorrect. Exact string match is appropriate for short categorical answers, not free-text summaries, since two good summaries will rarely match a reference word-for-word.
Incorrect. A binary PHI check evaluates a safety property, not whether the summary preserves the reference's key information and ordering.
